entries.name: Temporal-difference learning
entries.definition: A family of prediction-learning methods that assign temporal credit using discrepancies between successive, recursively related predictions of future outcomes, with intervening costs or rewards included when the target is cumulative.
entries.identity_notes: This family-level record covers temporal-difference prediction and the original TD(lambda) construction, including TD(0) and TD(1) endpoints. It is not a policy optimizer, the GAE advantage estimator, backpropagation as a way to compute derivatives, a Markov-chain model, or every sequential prediction problem. TD(lambda) is treated here as a specified family member rather than a synonym for the whole paradigm. No normalized identity match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 298 preceding native IDs/names/aliases. Full-checkout fixed-string searches included ignored and hidden files in worktree and main, returning 20 and 20 lines respectively. All 17 unique hit contents were inspected: prior TD(lambda) and Q-routing leads, GAE and AntNet boundary statements, and their saved reports/reviews. These were references to methods rather than existing candidate records. Six exact AIO CLASS nodes with scoped synonyms/comments and outgoing edges and six native neighboring mechanisms were inspected. Absence is bounded to this snapshot and semantic neighborhood.
limitations: The prediction targets must obey the declared temporal recursion. Consecutive forecasts of different future events cannot simply be subtracted; Section 5.3 embeds fixed-horizon forecasts in a larger set of related predictions. Terminal-outcome and cumulative-outcome formulations use different terminal conventions.

The original linear TD(0) theorem is convergence in expected value for an absorbing Markov setting, linearly independent state observation vectors, and sufficiently small constant step size, with weight changes after each sequence. It is not an almost-sure convergence theorem for arbitrary online nonlinear networks or a finite-data guarantee; the proof appendix was not independently audited.

TD(1)’s fixed-weight per-sequence equivalence does not make all TD methods identical to Monte Carlo or supervised learning. Updating weights within a sequence changes predictions and traces; Section 5.2 warns against mixing predictions computed with inconsistent parameter versions.

Temporal credit assignment and structural backpropagation are compatible but distinct. The method family alone supplies neither a control policy nor an exploration strategy. No claim of universal accuracy, lower computation, or benchmark superiority is curated.

claims.statement: For the original terminal-outcome problem, predictions P_t=P(x_t,w) estimate the same eventual scalar outcome z and P_(m+1)=z. With weights held fixed within a sequence, compute increments Delta w_t=alpha*(P_(t+1)−P_t)*e_t, where e_t=sum_(k=1..t) lambda^(t−k)*grad_w P_k and 0<=lambda<=1; apply their sum after the sequence. The trace can be maintained recursively as e_t=grad_w P_t+lambda*e_(t−1). TD(0) uses only the current prediction gradient, whereas TD(1) gives the same per-sequence changes as the corresponding supervised outcome-error update under the fixed-weight convention. In the cumulative-outcome extension, replace the difference with c_(t+1)+P_(t+1)−P_t and set the terminal remaining prediction to zero. This is the source’s undiscounted cumulative formulation, not an implicit insertion of a discount factor. Intra-sequence weight updates are a separate extension requiring consistent parameter timing; simple algebraic equivalence at fixed weights does not establish equality of online trajectories.

entries.name: Sarsa
entries.definition: An on-policy temporal-difference control algorithm that updates the current state-action value toward the observed reward plus the discounted estimated value of the next action selected by the same behavior policy.
entries.identity_notes: This record specifies one-step Sarsa through the tabular control formulation. The historical Modified Connectionist Q-Learning report supplies the selected-next-action target in a broader neural and eligibility-trace method; its lambda=0 case shares the one-step error, but the entire trace-based neural method is not made an exact alias of this record. Sarsa(lambda), expected Sarsa, Q-learning and GAE have distinct scopes. The available Cambridge PDF bears a September 1994 cover and already mentions Sutton’s proposed SARSA name in footnote 3; the later book draft credits the name to Sutton (1996). These source statements are preserved without resolving the naming chronology. No normalized identity match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 298 preceding native IDs/names/aliases. Full-checkout fixed-string searches included ignored and hidden files in worktree and main, returning 20 and 20 lines respectively. All 17 unique hit contents were inspected: prior TD(lambda) and Q-routing leads, GAE and AntNet boundary statements, and their saved reports/reviews. These were references to methods rather than existing candidate records. Six exact AIO CLASS nodes with scoped synonyms/comments and outgoing edges and six native neighboring mechanisms were inspected. Absence is bounded to this snapshot and semantic neighborhood.
limitations: A persistently exploratory behavior policy changes the values being estimated; an exploratory next action can lower or raise the sampled target relative to another action. Greedy Sarsa and Q-learning can coincide on a transition, but such a special case does not equate the methods.

Convergence requires a specified setting, sampling policy and step-size assumptions. The inspected book draft attributes its tabular control convergence statement to personal communication, and the 1994 neural report discusses parameter sensitivity and missing general guarantees. Neither source is treated as an independently verified complete proof for arbitrary function approximation.

The September 2016 book draft is versioned as a draft. Its retrospective naming attribution differs from the SARSA footnote in the available 1994-covered report; no first-use date or explanation of that discrepancy is asserted.

claims.statement: Maintain Q(s,a), choose the current action A using the current policy derived from Q, execute it, and observe reward R and next state S_next. For a nonterminal next state, choose A_next from that same policy before updating, then set Q(S,A)=Q(S,A)+alpha*(R+gamma*Q(S_next,A_next)−Q(S,A)), using pre-update values. Carry the selected A_next forward as the next executed action; it is not replaced with a fresh sample after the update. For a terminal next state, the continuation value is zero and no next environment action is executed. Control improves the policy from Q while retaining its declared exploration rule, such as epsilon-greedy selection. The sample target uses the actual selected next action, not a maximum over actions and not an expectation over all policy actions. Rummery and Niranjan’s Eq.9 uses this error multiplied by an eligibility-weighted sum of neural-output gradients; at lambda=0 only the current gradient remains. That historical extension does not make neural networks or nonzero traces necessary for one-step tabular Sarsa.

entries.name: Q-routing
entries.definition: A distributed adaptive packet-routing algorithm that learns destination-specific delivery-time estimates by combining observed local queue and transmission delays with a neighboring node’s estimate of remaining delivery time.
entries.identity_notes: This record denotes Boyan and Littman’s original tabular Q-routing method. It minimizes predicted delivery time using local bootstrapped information, unlike AntNet’s measured complete forward-trip feedback and probabilistic routing-table reinforcement. The exploratory full-echo scheme is a distinct variant, not an unmentioned mandatory part of the baseline. A neural approximation was explored but is not the defining original representation. No normalized identity match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 298 preceding native IDs/names/aliases. Full-checkout fixed-string searches included ignored and hidden files in worktree and main, returning 20 and 20 lines respectively. All 17 unique hit contents were inspected: prior TD(lambda) and Q-routing leads, GAE and AntNet boundary statements, and their saved reports/reviews. These were references to methods rather than existing candidate records. Six exact AIO CLASS nodes with scoped synonyms/comments and outgoing edges and six native neighboring mechanisms were inspected. Absence is bounded to this snapshot and semantic neighborhood.
limitations: The greedy baseline has no deliberate exploration once its initial policy is established. Overestimated unused alternatives can remain stale, impeding rediscovery of shortcuts when load decreases; the source explicitly reports this weakness. Full echo changes the information and update scheme and may introduce oscillation under heavy traffic.

Queue-dependent delays, other adaptive routers and changing traffic make the environment nonstationary relative to a destination/neighbor table. The record imports no stationary tabular Q-learning convergence theorem, optimality certificate, loop-freedom guarantee or universal routing superiority.

The displayed interior-node update needs declared destination-boundary, initialization, tie-breaking, disconnected-network and message-delay conventions in an executable implementation. The method text does not fully specify all these cases, and a simulator or complete protocol is not supplied by this conceptual record.

Results come from a simplified discrete-event network simulation; the paper explicitly says it is not fully realistic. The neural-network experiments were inconclusive. No empirical performance claim or deployment validation is curated.

claims.statement: At node x, maintain Q_x(d,y), the estimated time to deliver a packet to destination d through neighbor y, including waiting in x’s queue. Route using the neighbor with the smallest current estimate. Upon sending the packet to y, obtain its estimate t=min_z Q_y(d,z). With observed waiting time q at x and link-transmission time s from x to y, update the used table entry by Q_x(d,y)_new=Q_x(d,y)+eta*(q+s+t−Q_x(d,y)). This is an asynchronous local cost backup; it uses a minimum because delivery times are costs and the displayed target has no discount factor. The baseline only updates the selected neighbor entry. The full-echo extension separately queries all neighbors and updates their estimates, under a simulation assumption that the extra queries do not themselves congest the network.

native_neighbors.name: Q-learning
native_neighbors.definition: A model-free reinforcement-learning method that incrementally updates action-value estimates toward an observed reward plus the discounted maximum estimated value of the next state’s actions.
native_neighbors.identity_notes: The record captures one-step Q-learning through the original finite tabular formulation and its explicitly conditional convergence statement. claims.statement: At each node maintain destination-specific next-hop probabilities summing to one and local statistics of experienced trip times, including mean, variance and a recent best time. Periodically launch forward ants with destinations biased by local data traffic. They share data queues, record visited nodes and elapsed times, and choose among unvisited neighbors whenever any are available, falling back to all neighbors only when all have already been visited. Within that eligible set, choices use routing probabilities plus an instantaneous queue-length heuristic. On revisiting a node, remove the cycle from memory; discard an ant if the cycle consumed more than half its current age. At the destination, create a backward ant carrying the recorded path; it returns along that path through higher-priority queues. At each visited node, use forward-trip elapsed times to update the destination’s local statistics and reinforce the neighbor leading forward toward that destination. Statistically good subpaths can also update their corresponding destinations. For a chosen forward neighbor f and reinforcement r in (0,1], set P_f_new=P_f+r*(1−P_f) and each other P_n_new=(1−r)*P_n. The inspected scoring scheme combines a recent-best-time ratio with a dispersion-based correction and a normalized nonlinear squash; it rewards a path relative to local traffic conditions. Data packets sample from a power-reweighted routing table, whereas forward ants also use queue heuristics. Updates are concurrent and local; measured forward times, not recursively bootstrapped estimates from downstream nodes, supply the feedback.
